deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the preceding pages Grothendieck is drafting additional axioms for derivators beyond the basic list (Der 1–Der 5). The provisional 'Der 6' (p.49) says that a square gamma in D(Delta^1 x Delta^1) is cartesian iff it is cocartesian. This is exactly the axiom now used to define a stable derivator. The variant 'Der 6'' concerns fibred categories over the span Q. This page draws out consequences of that axiom and how it behaves under shifting.

(1) Top diagram. A square gamma in D(Delta^1 x Delta^1) has vertices gamma(i,j) and is oriented with gamma(0,0) as the 'target' corner. The maps are:
- i_1: gamma(1,1) -> gamma(0,1) and i_0: gamma(1,0) -> gamma(0,0), which are parallel;
- j_1: gamma(1,1) -> gamma(1,0) and j_0: gamma(0,1) -> gamma(0,0), which are parallel.
For a cocartesian (homotopy pushout) square, 'i_1 iso => i_0 iso' and 'j_1 iso => j_0 iso': the cobase change of an isomorphism is an isomorphism. Dually, in a cartesian square isomorphisms are stable under base change. Under Der 6 both directions hold for bicartesian squares.

(2) Margin. One should also require the axiom for the induced (shifted) derivators D_I: J |-> D(I x J), for every I in Diag. That is, squares in D(I x Delta^1 x Delta^1) are cartesian iff cocartesian.

(3) Grothendieck says this last condition follows from the preceding one, i.e. from the property of (1): the 'cont.' (cartesian) side gives one implication and the cocartesian side gives the other. This holds provided one has a 'Lemma' (a crossed-out label reads 'associé Der 6'). The lemma: if xi is a span xi_a -> xi_0 <- xi_b with arrow j_0 an isomorphism, then the corresponding square is cocartesian (and i_0 is iso). Equivalently, the inverse image p^*eta of an object eta in D(U), where U = (0 -> a) ≅ Delta^1, along the projection p: Delta^1 x Delta^1 -> U is cocartesian. In words: a square constant in one direction is cocartesian, and this is compatible with the shifts by I.

(4) Proof sketch. It suffices to show that the adjunction morphism relating xi and p^*p_!(xi) is an isomorphism. Here p is induced by pr_1: Delta^1 x Delta^1 -> Delta^1, so it is a (co)fibration. Hence p_! (and p_*) can be computed fibre by fibre (base-change axiom Der 4), and isomorphisms are detected pointwise (Der 2). This reduces the claim to the statement that A = D(e) -> D^{iso}(Delta^1) is an equivalence of categories. The target is the full subcategory of objects of D(Delta^1) whose structure arrow is an isomorphism, and the functor is p^* for Delta^1 -> e. Grothendieck calls this 'forme de Der 3'.

Purpose: to make the stability axiom 'cartesian <=> cocartesian' robust, i.e. inherited by all shifted derivators. Its first consequences are the base-change properties of isomorphisms in bicartesian squares and the bicartesianness of degenerate (constant) squares. These are the first lemmas in the modern theory of stable derivators. The next page tests the corresponding statements in HOT (Hot_W), including a pi_0 criterion for a cartesian square to be cocartesian and the 'cube lemma'.
errors: The argument is only sketched; the reduction step is very compressed. To be a proof it needs the base-change axiom (Der 4) for the (op)fibration pr_1, conservativity (Der 2), and full faithfulness of p^*: D(e) -> D(Delta^1), which uses the fact that Delta^1 has a terminal object.

Calling the final equivalence D(e) ≃ D^{iso}(Delta^1) a 'form of Der 3' is loose: it is a consequence of Der 2 and Der 4 (Kan extension along a functor with a final or initial object), not of Der 3 (existence of adjoints) alone.

The lemma's hypothesis is stated ambiguously ('tel que j_0 soit un iso, dans ce cas i_0 ...'). The intended statement is presumably: a square with two parallel arrows invertible is cocartesian (and cartesian). As written it mixes hypothesis and conclusion.

The claim that the shifted-derivator condition 'results' from the preceding condition is not fully justified on the page. In the modern theory, shifting is automatic because (co)cartesianness in D_I is detected pointwise in I, which again uses Der 2 and Der 4.

ideas.what: Axiom that a square in D(Delta^1 x Delta^1) is cartesian iff cocartesian (Der 6, from the preceding page, developed here)
ideas.modern_name: Stable derivator / stable homotopy theory axiom (bicartesian = cartesian = cocartesian)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Heller (stable homotopy theories, 1997), Franke (1996), Keller (1991), Maltsiniotis (2001-07), M. Groth (2013, 'Derivators, pointed derivators and stable derivators')
ideas.where_published: Possibly touched on in the 'Les Dérivateurs' manuscript (c. 1990-91); unsure whether stability is formulated there

ideas.what: In a cocartesian square the cobase change of an isomorphism is an isomorphism; dually for cartesian squares
ideas.modern_name: Isomorphisms are stable under homotopy (co)base change in a derivator
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; formalized for derivators by Groth (2013)

ideas.what: The axiom must also hold for the shifted derivators D_I = D(I x -)
ideas.modern_name: Stability of (co)cartesianness / stability under shifting of derivators
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (shifted derivators in Les Dérivateurs), Cisinski, Groth

ideas.what: Lemma: the pullback along pr_1: Delta^1 x Delta^1 -> Delta^1 of an object of D(Delta^1) (a square constant in one direction) is cocartesian, proved fibrewise
ideas.modern_name: Squares with two parallel isomorphisms are bicartesian (Groth's lemma on constant squares)
ideas.usually_credited_to: M. Groth (2013) and the derivator folklore

missed.claim: Historical: within the 'Champs' notes (dated from 1982 on), Grothendieck formulates and starts developing the 'cartesian iff cocartesian' axiom for derivators, including its stability under shifting. The modern definition of stable derivators is usually credited to the 1990s and later (Heller, Franke, Keller, Maltsiniotis, Groth). If this page dates near 1983 and not the late 1980s, it is an early, independent appearance of the stability axiom in derivator form.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Priority and history of stable derivators and stable (∞-)categories. The mathematics itself is now standard.

deep.surprise_reason: The lemmas on this page are routine first steps in the theory of stable derivators. The mild interest is historical: the stability axiom (cartesian ⇔ cocartesian), compatibility with shifts, and degenerate-square lemmas appear in Grothendieck's notes possibly well before the published literature on stable derivators. Nothing here is mathematically new to a specialist.
transcription_corrections: Top diagram labels: j_0 on gamma(0,1) -> gamma(0,0); i (i.e. i_1) on gamma(1,1) -> gamma(0,1); j_1 on gamma(1,1) -> gamma(1,0); i_0 (written like 'i,') on gamma(1,0) -> gamma(0,0).
Margin should read approximately: 'De plus, on doit imposer [Der 6] pour les dérivateurs induits D_I (I ∈ Diag) [i.e.] dans D(I×Δ¹×Δ¹)'.
'(on cont. implique ⇒, ...)' is probably '(un cart. implique ⇒, un cocartésien implique ⇐)', i.e. cartesian and cocartesian each give one implication.
U = (0 → a) ≃ Δ¹ is written as the domain of p; the struck phrase after it is about the 'objet cocartésien'.
'Comme p est ...' is probably 'Comme p est bien cofibrant [or 'fibrant'], comme induit par pr_1: Δ¹×Δ¹ → Δ¹'.
The target category written D^{xx}(Δ¹) probably denotes the full subcategory of D(Δ¹) of objects whose arrow is an isomorphism (e.g. D^{is}(Δ¹)), not D^{cc}.
The bottom line reads approximately 'que A = D(e) → D^{..}(Δ¹) est une équiv. de cat. (forme de Der 3)*'.
